extracted.intended_audience: general readers; writers, scholars, critics, and fans of science fiction interested in the cyberpunk genre
extracted.subtask_description: Describing the characteristics, themes, settings, tropes, style, and social/political stance that define the cyberpunk subgenre of science fiction; useful for writers, critics, and scholars who need a checklist of what constitutes cyberpunk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowlife and high tech
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberpunk is characterized by its focus on a combination of 'lowlife and high tech'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize contrast between advanced technologies (AI, cyberware, virtual reality) and degraded social conditions or marginal lives. Example works: Neuromancer, Blade Runner. The phrase captures the core tension a story should explore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Near-future, Earth-bound setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots tend to be set in a near-future Earth, rather than in far-future settings or galactic vistas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lean toward plausible, recognizable technological extrapolations and urban landscapes rather than space opera or distant futures. Keeps stakes grounded and socially immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-industrial dystopia and urban landscapes
rubrics_metrics.description: Settings are usually post-industrial dystopias and often urbanized, artificial landscapes (cityscapes, 'city lights, receding').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyper-urbanization, decayed infrastructure, crowded slums (e.g., inspiration from Kowloon Walled City, Hong Kong panoramas) to evoke the genre's ambience and socio-economic contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict among AI, hackers, and megacorporations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberpunk plots often involve conflict between artificial intelligence, hackers, and megacorporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct antagonisms driven by corporate power, networked intelligences, and marginalized tech-savvy protagonists; make institutional power and digital systems central to plot dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invasive cyberware and human augmentation (transhumanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features invasive modification of the human body, cyberware, transhumanism and technologically augmented humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray ethical, identity, and social consequences of augmentation. Trope examples: neural implants, brain–computer links, cyborg bodies; examine personal and societal tensions that arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyberspace and virtual reality tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the action can take place online or in 'cyberspace', blurring line between actual and virtual reality; including direct connections between the human brain and computer systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include immersive or sensory VR, hacking-as-plot-device, and the consequences of living through mediated realities. Use metaphors and sensory detail to render virtual spaces vividly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noir/detective influences and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmosphere often echoes film noir and uses techniques from detective fiction; the genre frequently adopts a hardboiled or tech-noir tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt morally ambiguous protagonists, investigative structures, terse or evocative prose, and visual/atmospheric descriptions reminiscent of noir cinema (e.g., Blade Runner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character archetype: marginalized, alienated loners
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic cyberpunk characters were marginalized, alienated loners who lived on the edge of society in generally dystopic futures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make protagonists outsiders or antiheroes whose marginality gives them distinctive perspectives on power, technology, and society; avoid idealized heroes firmly embedded in institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on style, surfaces, and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cyberpunk writing emphasizes style, a fascination with surfaces, and atmosphere over traditional science-fiction tropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize evocative scene-setting, sensory detail, and voice (William Gibson's approach) rather than exhaustive technical exposition; mood and aesthetic coherence are central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socio-political critique: corporate oligarchy and late capitalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberpunk often depicts governments weakened or overshadowed by wealthy corporate elites and serves as a critique of late capitalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame institutions and economic structures as sources of oppression or systemic dysfunction; use corporate power and commodification as thematic drivers rather than neutral background elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural rebellion and countercultural ethos
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberpunk often expresses a sense of rebellion and suggests a cultural revolution in science fiction, aligning with punk attitudes and hacker subculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse narratives with anti-authoritarian sensibilities, subcultural aesthetics, DIY/hacker ethics, and skepticism of mainstream values; the aesthetic should feel iconoclastic or subversive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tropes and motifs (AI, megacorp, cybercrime, virtual reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common tropes include artificial intelligence, cyberware, megacorporations, virtual reality, cybercrime, and the 'datasphere' of computerized information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these motifs organically to serve theme/plot rather than as checklist items. Example media: Neuromancer, Ghost in the Shell, Cyberpunk 2077.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'street finds its own uses for things' ethos
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies are shown being repurposed by society in unexpected ways—the street finds its own uses for things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict grassroots adaptation, bricolage, and unintended social uses of tech; show how user behavior transforms designed systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and lineage (New Wave, punk, hacker culture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre's origins and legitimacy are tied to influences from New Wave SF, punk subculture, early hacker culture, Beat authors, and authors like Philip K. Dick and William Gibson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for 'classic' cyberpunk authenticity, acknowledge or weave in elements traceable to these influences—experimental prose, countercultural references, and technological paranoia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese cyberpunk distinctives
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese cyberpunk has roots in underground music and punk subculture and often manifests differently (anime/manga aesthetics, different cultural sources such as Akira, Ghost in the Shell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in or drawing from Japanese cyberpunk traditions, emphasize visceral, body-focused imagery, punk-influenced aesthetics, and the specific cultural interplay of modern Japan with tech imagery; avoid flattening or misrepresenting cultural particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation pitfalls and critique (techno-Orientalism, marginalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note cyberpunk's tendency to marginalize women and people of colour and to employ techno-Orientalist or racist tropes in portrayals of East Asia and Asians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of representation: avoid exoticizing cultures or using them merely as dystopian scenery; develop diverse, complex characters and avoid reinforcing stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative subgenres and focus shifts (biopunk, postcyberpunk, solarpunk)
rubrics_metrics.description: As cyberpunk themes spread, derivative subgenres emerged (biopunk, steampunk, solarpunk, postcyberpunk) that reorient focus (e.g., biotechnology vs. information technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which subgenre you're working in; adjust central technologies, ethical questions, and aesthetics accordingly to avoid genre drift or incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and adaptation conventions (film, anime, games, RPGs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberpunk frequently appears across media—literature, film, television, anime/manga, video games, tabletop RPGs—each with its own conventions and affordances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt genre elements to the medium: games may foreground player agency and open worlds (e.g., Cyberpunk 2077), film emphasizes visual tech-noir aesthetics, while prose can explore interiority and ambiguous voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/branding constraint: trademarked term
rubrics_metrics.description: In some jurisdictions 'Cyberpunk' is a registered trademark (e.g., owned by CD Projekt SA in the U.S.; split ownership in the EU).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'Cyberpunk' as a product or brand name, check trademark status in the relevant jurisdiction; as a genre descriptor in criticism or fiction it remains widely used but commercial naming may require licensing or alternate phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and narrative technique (updated Chandleresque voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cyberpunk narration echoes older hardboiled voices (e.g., Gibson's voice resembling Raymond Chandler) and often privileges distinctive, immediate narrative voice over exhaustive exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a stylistic voice that balances terse, evocative prose with technological detail; avoid clumsy info-dumps and prefer sensory, scene-based revelation of worldbuilding.
